title: Finding a Place for Social Work in Public Service - unh.edu
content: Ben Goguen ’27 was looking for an internship that would give him experience working in government without losing the people-centered focus of his social work education. He found that opportunity as a congressional intern for U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen in Manchester, NH. A social work and justice studies dual major, Goguen spent his summer speaking with constituents, conducting grant and policy research, drafting correspondence, and attending events with Shaheen. The experience showed Goguen how well his two majors complement each other. While social work has prepared him to understand and assist individuals and communities, justice studies has helped him understand how laws, policies, and systems shape their lives. Together, he says, they have prepared him to approach issues from both individual and systemic perspectives in government, policy, advocacy and public service. “I would also encourage students to explore different fields and interests alongside social work,” Goguen says. “You never know which experience will help you find the type of work you are most passionate about. For me, working in government has shown me that I can still use the values and skills I have learned through social work while working toward change on a larger scale.” Every day in the senator’s office was a little different. My main role was answering constituent phone calls, which generally fell into two categories: policy and legislative comments or constituent services. Constituents would call in support of or opposition to legislation, and my role was to document their position and any relevant comments. Constituent service cases ranged from urgent issues like homelessness or eviction to Granite Staters stranded overseas who needed assistance returning to the United States. While manning the phones, I typically had an event letter or grant support letter I was drafting. When the Senate is in session, the senator is primarily in D.C., so if she was unable to attend an event in New Hampshire, I would draft a letter on her behalf to be read by a staff member. I also drafted letters supporting federal grant applications from organizations and departments across the state. Another amazing aspect of the internship was attending events alongside the senator around the state. She has always made visiting Granite Staters a priority, and getting to join her in interacting with constituents and their businesses was incredibly meaningful. Meeting Sen. Shaheen for the first time. We were at an event in Merrimack, and after shaking my hand and asking me a few questions, she gave me a shout-out in front of everyone at the event. I was wearing UNH colors (navy suit, blue and gray tie), of course, and she told everyone about how much she loves both UNH and her interns. Outside of that, I loved hearing success stories from the casework team. Often, I would be the first point of contact for constituents calling for urgent assistance, so hearing months later that they received the help they needed was incredibly rewarding. Seeing how the senator’s office was able to help people going through dark times made the hard work worth it. Immigration issues and housing insecurity are some of the most common things Granite Staters need help with at the federal level. Many days were hard and included very emotional calls for help, but each call taught me so much about the issues people are actually facing. Through working with constituents, I learned that no case is the same. Everyone has their own story, and there is often so much more going on in someone’s life than what we see on the surface. A housing issue is not just about finding a place to live, and an immigration case is not just about paperwork or waiting for a decision. These issues impact people’s families, jobs, financial stability, mental well-being, and their ability to plan for the future. This experience has made me much more aware of the human side of policy and government. Behind every law, program, agency, and statistic are real people impacted by the decisions being made. It has also shown me just how important constituent services are. This work may not always make headlines, but helping someone navigate a federal agency or resource, or simply feel heard, can make a meaningful difference in their life. That is something I will carry with me as I continue pursuing a career in public service. SW 625: SW Policy-Activism & Advocacy, taught by Meredith Young, was the most impactful class I have taken at UNH and really covers the role of social workers at a macro, community-wide level. Understanding how to ethically work with clients while being aware of how policy and legislation impact people’s lives is imperative for the work of a social worker. In addition, the roleplays in both my SW 622 and SW 623 practice courses prepared me well for my interactions with constituents this summer. The NASW values for social work were always at the forefront of my mind when speaking with and advocating for constituents, and I can confidently say that de-escalation techniques covered in my social work education came in handy. Working in a congressional office showed me how the same social work values that are used when working directly with clients can be applied at the policy and advocacy levels. Whether I was speaking with a constituent about a policy or listening to someone explain a difficult situation, I was still using social work skills rooted in empathy, advocacy and meeting people where they are. This experience has shown me that being a social worker does not have to mean working in a traditional social work setting. It can also mean working to make systems and policies better serve the people who depend on them. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Coming Up Dry - unh.edu
content: At the end of a dry summer, John Moulton ’74, of Moulton Farm in Meredith, looks at his irrigation pond. Though it’s down from the high-water mark, there’s still plenty of water for him to draw. He says that’s due to changes in irrigation and planting strategies promoted by UNH Extension, including the use of drip irrigation placed under a biodegradable mulch. If he were still relying on overhead watering, as he did when he first started, his pond would be dry by now. “We’ve been irrigating many of our crops, and right now we’re still looking at 8 or 900,000 gallons of water out of a total capacity of 1.2 million,” Moulton says. “Years ago, we would have drained that pond by this time.” Moulton’s need for a new approach to irrigation, shared by farmers and gardeners across the state, is a result of a dry 2026. It can no longer be called abnormally dry, though, because weather data show dry summers are becoming more common in New England. Though not traditionally thought of as a dry climate, recent experience has shown that drought is no longer a rare event in New Hampshire. The state’s Department of Environmental Services reports that drought occurred 11 times between 2000 and 2020, and that as of August of 2026, parts of Rockingham and Strafford counties have been experiencing moderate drought for 12 months and counting. It is time for New Englanders to bone up on gardening in drought conditions. The irrigation pond at Moulton Farm in Meredith holds about 1.2 million gallons of water. While the effects of dry conditions are most apparent above ground, as leaves wilt and stems droop, some of the more concerning things are happening at the plant’s roots. “There are several layers of how drought impacts soil and plant health,” says Renuka Mathur, UNH Extension’s soil health state specialist. To explain drought’s effects on soil, Mathur starts by noting specific elements of soil, including organic matter, as well as the mycorrhizal fungus and microbes that decompose the organic residue and make nutrients available to nearby roots. Dry conditions can reduce the activity of fungus and microbes, making for less nutrient availability to plants. Prolonged drought can kill off the fungus and microbes, meaning that soil will be less active when moisture returns. “If fungus and microbes die, they don’t bounce back immediately,” Mathur says. It can take several seasons, she adds, and the mix of microbes might be different when they do return. “Sometimes the damage of the drought can be permanent.” If the microbes and fungi aren’t delivering nutrition, it might be tempting to use fertilizers, Mathur says, but doing so in drought conditions comes with hazards. Without rainfall and accompanied by high temperatures, the fertilizer, typically applied as a salt compound, can concentrate on leaves or the soil surface, leading to burn injuries for the plant. “If you want to fertilize, do so in the evening or early morning so the salt injury risk is reduced,” Mathur says. She also warns against excessive tilling, because it exposes more moisture to evaporation, and has other negative effects. “When you till dry soil, it breaks the structure of the soil and causes rapid decomposition of organic residue in the soil,” Mathur says. “Add a little bit of rain or wind, and it causes fine disrupted soil to re-settle, creating a cementing effect. It does so in a dense layer that prevents water absorption and encourages water and nutrient runoff.” Instead of tilling, Mathur suggests mulching — placing a layer of some material on top of the soil, often done as a weed control measure. Mulch also has the benefit of keeping moisture levels higher in the soil. If there were a mulch fan club, Sean O’Brien, home horticulture program manager for Extension, could campaign to be its president. “I advocate for mulch all the time, for lots of reasons but certainly moisture loss is a big one,” O’Brien says. He suggests using “whatever you have abundantly” to mulch, whether it’s fallen leaves, straw, pine needles, or even cardboard. Many commercial growers will use plastic, but home growers might prefer a material that will break down in the soil at the end of the growing season and become next year’s organic matter. The presence of organic matter in soil will help it to retain moisture. O’Brien says they recommend organic matter content of 4 to 10%, and Extension offers soil testing for those who want to know precisely. While you’re mulching, it might be a good time to think about your irrigation strategy. Watering with a sprinkler or by hand is the easiest to set up, but “overhead watering,” as O’Brien terms it, is problematic. Some of the water evaporates before it’s absorbed by the soil, it can encourage disease spread through splashing, and is often associated with under-watering. Drip irrigation or soaker hoses, ideally placed underneath the mulch layer, ensure that the water goes where the roots can reach it — while minimizing water use.To that point, O’Brien says that irrigation frequency and volume are important considerations. Water less often, but soak the soil when you do, he says, which will train your plants to grow long roots. “You want to make sure you’re watering deeply and less frequently, that will help your plants to weather those drier conditions.” When planning your garden, select plant varieties that are drought resistant, says. O’Brien, who notes that there are varieties of just about every plant that can handle a dry spell. “Drought is something that we’re going to have to deal with for the foreseeable future,” O’Brien says.“For gardeners, it’s the new frontier.” Regular and extended drought might be a new problem for New Hampshire gardeners. Thankfully, local gardeners have adaptability — as well as expertise from UNH Extension — to keep their gardens green. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Unlocking the Outdoors - unh.edu
content: Everyone should be able to take a stroll — or a roll — through the woods in New Hampshire, believe the folks behind the website Trail Finder. For those who have ability limitations, though, starting down a trail can be a gamble, as it’s hard to know exactly what kind of terrain is around the next bend. The odds are turning in their favor, thanks to a partnership between UNH Extension and Trail Finder. As a result of that partnership, Brendan Thornton ’27 spent his summer surveying and documenting the accessibility of trails throughout the state. Thornton gathered data on 29 trails this year, bringing the total number of surveyed trails to 56 so far. Trail Finder’s effort to make trails more welcoming to more people began several years ago, when they added the ability for trails to be marked as “accessible.” That was a solution that invited more questions than it answered, they found. The problem with the initial strategy used by Trail Finder’s designers, said Stephen Engle, executive director of Community Geographics, a digital mapping technology company that joined with Extension and the Upper Valley Trails Alliance to create the platform in 2010, was that it used a simplistic approach to accessibility. In that first attempt, a trail network was considered either accessible or not, and it was left up to the trail owner or manager to make the call. Results were uneven at best, Engle says. A trail might be listed as accessible even though there was a curb between the parking lot and trail head. Or, in other cases, a largely accessible network was not marked as such because the trail manager felt uncertain. “On the whole, we felt that Trail Finder wasn’t doing the best job in helping users find trails to meet their ability,” says Engle. They needed a new approach, one that leans into the quirks and features of each individual trail. Each trail has its own aspects of accessibility, such as incline, trail surface, and restroom facilities. Each hiker has their unique physical limitations, and a trail that’s accessible to one person might be hazardous for someone else. “Everybody has their own perception. There are differing interpretations of what accessible means.” When talking about barriers to trail access, says UNH Extension Specialist Emma Tutein, a lack of information might be the first hurdle. “Where is the trail, what is it like, how do we even get to it?” Tutein says. “For a lot of people, they want to know. And that becomes more important if you have a disability.” The problem is, gathering all that data takes time and expertise. A solution was found in 2025 when a UNH student, interning with Extension, spent his summer examining trails for their surface material, width, degree of incline, cross-slope, and amenities such as benches and accessible restrooms. The NH Charitable Foundation provides funding for the project. This summer, that cache of information doubled in size, thanks to the efforts of Brendan Thornton ’27, an environmental conservation and sustainability major who has been exploring New Hampshire woods since he was a toddler. “This job is cool because I get to use my love for nature and the outdoors ,” Thornton says, “and apply my skills to helping people who might not have the same opportunities as me.” One of Thornton’s relatives has Down syndrome, so he already understood the importance of inclusion. Working on the trail project gave him new insight, however. He was studying a trail in North Conway when a man stopped and told him about his wife, who has trouble navigating certain trails due to nerve damage, although her disability is invisible to most. “Knowing that I’m helping people like that is pretty cool,” Thornton says. “It’s definitely something I think about when I’m out there.” Engle says that people with disabilities are used to encountering physical barriers, but sometimes informational barriers are the hardest to overcome. No one wants to make it halfway down a trail only to find an unexpected stream crossing, gate or boulder blocking their progress. “One of the most important things for us to understand is that having detailed information about trails benefits everyone. But we haven’t taken the time to curate our trails to the levels that people really needed,” Engle says. That’s now changing, he adds, with the growing list of trail networks that are built, or re-built, to be accessible to all users. And it’s also changing through the work of people like Thornton, who says he wants everyone to be able to access the benefits of trail walking. “It slows me down and it makes me appreciate what’s going on around me,” Thornton says. “It’s a place where there’s no noise, your head’s clear, and you don’t have anything going on except looking around to see nature’s beauty. That experience should be accessible to everyone.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Why Is UNH Stock Trading At A Premium With The Slowest Growth? - Trefis
content: UnitedHealth (UNH) runs the best operating margin of the three managed care companies in its peer group, and the slowest revenue growth of the three. It also carries a significant valuation premium over its peer, Cigna, trading at more than double its earnings multiple. The headline margin spread reflects UnitedHealth’s higher-margin Optum services mix as much as underwriting efficiency. What the current valuation assumes is that this consolidated edge holds. The size of the premium is clearest against Cigna. UnitedHealth trades at 25.6 times trailing net earnings on a 4.8% operating margin—though its raised 2026 guidance brings that multiple closer to 21 times forward earnings. Cigna trades at 11.3 times trailing net earnings on 3.2%. CVS trades at 25.1 times, but on trailing earnings that include at least one loss quarter, so it does not compare with a clean year. The premium is not buying revenue growth. UnitedHealth’s revenue grew 6.5% over the last twelve months, the slowest in the group, against Cigna’s 7.7%. Nor is the premium buying the group’s highest trailing return—CVS delivered 34.3% against UnitedHealth’s 30.5%—even as both soundly beat the S&P 500’s managed care index over the same stretch. The stock also sits about 33% below its two-year high. Not only in the health plan. UnitedHealthcare is guided to at least $12 billion of operating earnings for 2026, against about $25.45 billion guided for the whole company. Revenue over the trailing twelve months was $450.13 billion, the base the 4.8% trailing margin is measured against, and the 2026 guidance is what shows where those earnings come from. The lead is earned beside the insurance book as well as inside it. The rest sits in Optum. Optum Rx, the pharmacy benefit business, is guided to $6.25 billion of operating earnings for 2026 on its own, and management has been rebuilding it around monthly per-member fees. Management expects to end 2026 with more than 95% of clients on full pass-through of manufacturer rebates. Optum Health, the care delivery arm, cares for 20 million people through primary and specialist care, ambulatory surgery and home health. Management raised its 2026 adjusted earnings per share guidance to a range of $19.50 to $20.00, up from greater than $18.25. The test is the second half of 2026, now underway, when earnings tilt heavily toward Optum Rx and Optum Insight to make up for UnitedHealthcare’s front-loaded year. The pressure sits in the commercial book. Management says medical cost trends there are running modestly above 11%, higher than planned, and full commercial margin recovery to its target 7%-plus range remains pushed past 2027, as management previously indicated. One driver is the arbitration process under the No Surprises Act, which management says is adding about 50 basis points of incremental cost trend in 2026, with management noting that roughly 60% of cases are driven by just five entities. UnitedHealthcare is opening its front door wider at the same time. From October 1 a broad range of conditions no longer needs prior approval, part of a plan to eliminate 30% of its prior authorization volume by the end of 2026. At 25.6 times earnings, the stock’s valuation prices in a margin lead that the commercial book is still working to recover, paired with the group’s slowest top-line growth. On September 3, a caller asked if UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (NYSE:UNH) has enough profitable growth that they should consider adding it to their portfolio. Mad Money host Jim Cramer replied: Yes, the answer: it does, it does. You know, I've got to tell you, I thought that last quarter was very, very good. The stock market did not like the quarter as much as I thought it would, but the stock's making a stand here. I think that UNH is good to buy. Cramer's bullish stance rests on the core strength of the company's financial delivery and improving execution. In its second-quarter 2026 report, UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (NYSE:UNH) posted consolidated revenues of $112 billion and operating earnings of $8 billion. Adjusted diluted earnings per share reached $6.38, outpacing Wall Street expectations by $1.48. Driven by strong performance across both the UnitedHealthcare and Optum divisions, management raised its full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to a range of $19.50 to $20. Furthermore, the medical care ratio improved to 86.7% down from 89.4% a year prior, showing that medical cost trends and pricing are aligning effectively. On the other hand, Wall Street remains cautious about lingering cost pressures across the managed care landscape. Even though the medical care ratio improved compared to last year, patients continuing to utilize medical services at a high rate keeps expenses heavy. At the same time, commercial insurance margins are taking longer to bounce back. Adding in tighter payment adjustments for government-backed plans along with heavy spending on tech infrastructure, cautious investors could have reasons to wait rather than chasing the stock higher. Insider Monkey's data tracking over 1000 hedge funds shows accumulation by major asset managers. 143 hedge funds had positions in UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (NYSE:UNH) in Q2 compared to 130 in Q1. Of those funds, Fisher Asset Management was the top shareholder with nearly 9.1 million shares. The firm increased its position in the stock by 74% in the quarter. Additionally, short interest remains low, with the short percentage of the float sitting at 1.92%, showing a general lack of aggressive bearish bets against the stock. title: Are There Links Between Dairy Consumption and Depression? - unh.edu
content: Depression is a complex disease that can be difficult to identify, but nearly one in five Americans has received a diagnosis for depression and one in 20 are affected by depression symptoms on a daily basis. A wide variety of factors can underlie depression and depressive symptoms, but new research at UNH indicates that dairy products do not contribute to worse depressive symptoms in a group of people previously documented to be at a particularly high risk for depression. It further suggests that yogurt and butter in particular may be beneficial. Consumption of dairy products with higher fat content, including yogurt and butter, was associated with fewer depressive symptoms. Dairy consumption is recommended as part of a healthy diet by the U.S. Dietary Guidelines for Americans. Dairy includes a unique profile of fatty acids, along with other nutrients, that may benefit inflammation. There is concern over the recommendation of consuming full-fat dairy products, however, due to saturated fat content. Yet the potential impacts of dairy, including those with fat, on depression, a leading cause of poor quality of life, is limited. A study published in Nutrients and led by Sherman Bigornia, associate professor in the Department of Agriculture, Nutrition, and Food Systems in the College of Life Sciences and Agriculture (COLSA), looked at the association of total dairy consumption as well as individual dairy products — milk, cheese, yogurt, cream, and butter — with depressive symptoms in Hispanic/Latino adults over a six-year period. The team, which included researchers from nine institutions, used data from the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL), an ongoing longitudinal study of 16,415 Hispanic/Latino adults living in the U.S. Evidence suggests Hispanic/Latino adults experience high rates of depression, and they also have a disproportionate burden of obesity and metabolic syndrome, both characterized by chronic inflammation. Chronic inflammation, cardiovascular dysfunction, and metabolic syndrome have all been implicated in depression. Researchers from HCHS/SOL collected participants’ baseline dietary information and also assessed depressive symptoms using a validated survey scale at the initial visit and again during a follow-up clinical exam six years later. A total of 10,618 participants provided complete data for analysis. The Bigornia team, including first author Anne Bodenrader ’26G, used the data to identify and estimate daily dairy product consumption and analyzed associations with depressive symptoms. The team found that total dairy consumption was not significantly associated with depressive symptoms over the six-year period. Individual dairy products showed some potentially important differences, however. While milk, cheese, and cream consumption were not significantly associated with the score, yogurt and butter consumption were both significantly associated with fewer depressive symptoms. The effect sizes were very small, underscoring the need for cautious interpretation and further study, but both yogurt and butter have biological properties that make beneficial effects plausible. title: UnitedHealth Slips 3% as TPG Buys Into Florida WellMed Clinics Ahead of Guidance Reaffirmation - 24/7 Wall St.
content: TPG just bought into the exact Optum clinics that derailed UnitedHealth's profits, and management is hours away from reaffirming guidance that could either validate the deal or reopen a wound investors hoped was healing. UnitedHealth Group (NYSE:UNH | UNH Price Prediction) stock is down 3% to $388.58 in early Wednesday trading after Bloomberg reported the company sold an interest in part of its Florida WellMed primary-care clinics. The 3% slide comes even as UnitedHealth stock is still up 15% year to date, and it lands hours before management is set to reaffirm full-year 2026 financial guidance at an investor conference, according to UnitedHealth Group. TPG (NASDAQ:TPG) is the buyer. The Fort Worth alternative asset manager ended Q2 2026 with $326.8 billion in assets under management and $76.2 billion in available capital, and its Capital and Healthcare Partners platforms have been active in senior-care buyouts. WellMed sits inside Optum Health, the value-based care unit whose stumbles drove UnitedHealth’s ongoing turnaround. The reaction today looks company-specific rather than sector-wide, and that framing matters for anyone reading through from UnitedHealth into the broader managed-care group. Bloomberg reported Tuesday evening that UnitedHealth sold an interest in some of its Optum Health operations in Florida to TPG, centered on WellMed’s senior primary-care clinics. Terms weren’t disclosed, which leaves investors valuing a transaction with no headline dollar figure attached to it. Chief Financial Officer Wayne DeVeydt told Bloomberg, “We didn’t need the dollars, we have the dollars to invest, but we needed the focus and somebody that could actually work with us locally.” He described the arrangement as a way to grow the clinic footprint faster than UnitedHealth could on its own while it executes a wider reset. DeVeydt also told the outlet that Optum Health margins will reach 2% this year, ahead of prior expectations, and he guided to 4% next year. That trajectory matters because Optum Health was the source of last year’s disappointing profit and the reason the company replaced its chief executive and other senior leaders. UnitedHealth reported Optum Health revenue of $23.47 billion in Q2 2026, down 5% year over year (YoY) as the unit shed 700,000 value-based care patients. title: How to Start a Career in Real Estate Before Graduation - unh.edu
content: Amanda Clifford ’26 works at her desk at the Residences on Madison in Worcester, Mass. Are you interested in a career in real estate but unsure which path might be right for you? Recent UNH Paul College alum Amanda Clifford made her way into the profession by focusing on entrepreneurial studies and pairing it with the real estate finance and investments minor. During her final semester, Clifford interned with CP Management. When the company learned she would be moving back home to Shrewsbury, Mass., after graduation, an opportunity emerged at a nearby property. Before graduating, Clifford had accepted a full-time position as leasing manager at the Residences on Madison, a new property managed by CP Management in Worcester. “Entrepreneurial studies complemented the real estate finance and investments minor because it taught me to look at real estate from more than just one perspective. The minor gave me more of the technical and industry-specific knowledge, while my major taught me how to recognize opportunities, think creatively, solve problems, and understand what goes into running and growing a business,” Clifford says. "I think that combination has shaped how I look at my career. Rather than feeling like I have to follow one specific path within real estate, I’m interested in gaining experience in different areas of the industry and eventually using what I learn to create opportunities for myself.” Clifford discusses how her UNH experience and internship helped launch her career in real estate and shape where she hopes to take it next. I helped the company internally by updating files in its shared drive, developing marketing ideas for specific properties, and conducting market research. I also worked on-site at one of the properties the company managed. There, I mainly helped with administrative tasks, but I was able to watch the leasing process from start to finish, which was helpful when I started my current job. I was able to watch real estate professionals do their jobs and see how they interact and what goes into being a property manager. I learned how to communicate with residents, vendors, and coworkers, how to handle problems as they come up, and how much goes into keeping a property running day to day. I also had the opportunity to attend networking events and see a different side of the industry. My job is to bring in prospective residents, give tours, review applications, and get leases signed. I also run the company's social media accounts. Once someone moves in and becomes a resident, they work with the property manager. Anything before that is my responsibility. Taking the Real Estate Finance course was beneficial. I learned a lot about how the real estate industry works, including how to conduct market research and property analyses and build pro formas. Taking classes before starting my internship helped me understand that real estate is about much more than buying and selling houses. Watching property managers in action and attending networking events during my internship showed me how many facets there are to the industry and how many different career opportunities there are to explore. I've always been interested in real estate because of the freedom and flexibility it can provide, both financially and in terms of different career paths. I've always seen myself working in real estate, whether full time, on the side, or something I pick up later in life. When I saw the new minor, I realized I had already taken many of the required courses and knew it would be beneficial to me in some capacity. The experience helped me narrow down my future plans and goals in ways I didn't realize I needed. I genuinely don't know where I'd be right now had I not pursued the minor and internship. I certainly wouldn't have as clear an idea of where I want to take the next five years or where I want to be in my career. I had no idea it would help provide me with the opportunity to have a full-time job lined up before graduating! I don’t necessarily have one specific position or path that I’m set on, and I think that’s partly because there are so many different directions I could take within real estate. My biggest goal is to keep gaining experience, learn as much as I can, and become financially stable enough to have more freedom in the choices I make. I also hope to have started taking steps toward working for myself in some capacity, whether that’s through real estate, entrepreneurship, or a combination of the two. I know ultimately, I want to build a business of my own. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

content: Melanie Carolan is researching something of a moving target. Carolan, a doctoral student in natural resources and Earth systems science, is studying the New Hampshire and Maine coast from above the waterline in an attempt to accurately map a coastline that doesn’t necessarily look the same from one day to the next. The nearshore waters she studies present unique challenges, making them particularly difficult to map: Tides shift the shoreline, navigation hazards make boat surveys risky, and the habitats themselves are easily disturbed. But Carolan is working with Jennifer Dijkstra, research assistant professor, and a broader research team to use technology to overcome some of those challenges. Her research utilizes a combination of several remote sensing systems, including aerial drones that map seaweeds and boating hazards, to fill in the mapping picture. Better nearshore data means better information for coastal navigation, construction and conservation In her previous work, Carolan used remote underwater video systems to track where fish, crabs and lobsters live and move, addressing gaps in fishery-independent monitoring data as species distributions shift. "The coolest aspect is that it's a highly visual form of research," Carolan says. "I get to see seals swimming, fish schooling and birds diving while analyzing the footage." Carolan’s research has been funded by a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) award to UNH, with additional support from New Hampshire Sea Grant Development Funds.
